issues.legal_issue: A law abolishing intermediary land interests by transferring them to the State is a law concerning acquisition of property rather than land and land tenures.
material_facts: The Act transferred proprietors’ and tenure-holders’ interests in estates and related property to the State in order to eliminate intermediaries and bring occupants into direct relations with the Government.
issues.conclusion: The Act was, in substance, a law concerning acquisition of property under entry 36 of List II, not a law concerning land and land tenures under entry 18 of List II.
issues.legal_principle: The legislative entries are construed according to the substance and dominant object of the law. The Court distinguished entry 18 from entry 36 of List II; acquisition of property is specifically covered by entry 36. The entries are heads of legislative power, not sources of implied restrictions.

predicates.state_legislation_challenged: A party challenged the validity of a State law in court.
predicates.dominant_object_transfers_land_interests: The law’s dominant object is to transfer land-related proprietary interests from intermediaries to the State.

issues.definition: When a challenged State law principally transfers land-related proprietary interests to the State, it is classified as a property-acquisition law.

issues.legal_issue: The constitutional power to acquire property does not itself carry an implied obligation to provide compensation, and a protected acquisition law cannot be challenged for failing to provide or adequately provide compensation.
material_facts: The challenged law authorized acquisition of estates and specified a compensation scheme that the proprietors argued was illusory or inadequate.
The legislation was pending in the State Legislature when the Constitution commenced, received the President’s assent, and was included in the constitutional schedule protecting specified laws.
issues.conclusion: The compensation obligation does not arise by implication from the legislative entries on acquisition or compensation; the challenge to the adequacy or absence of compensation was barred by the constitutional protections applicable to the Act.
issues.legal_principle: Article 31(2) expressly imposes the compensation requirement, while entries 36 of List II and 42 of List III are legislative heads and do not independently impose that duty. Article 31(4) bars challenges to a qualifying law on the ground that it contravenes article 31(2); articles 31-A and 31-B protect the specified acquisition laws from challenges based on Part III. In Sankari Prasad Singh Deo v. Union of India, the Court upheld the First Amendment that inserted articles 31-A and 31-B. The Court held that Julius v. Bishop of Oxford does not make a legislative entry a power coupled with a duty to legislate.

rule.if: acquisition_law_challenge and (challenge_based_on_missing_or_inadequate_compensation) and (pending_at_constitution_start and presidential_assent and constitutionally_protected_law)

predicates.acquisition_law_challenge: A party challenged a law authorizing compulsory acquisition of property.
predicates.challenge_based_on_missing_or_inadequate: The challenger claimed that the law failed to provide compensation or provided inadequate compensation.
predicates.pending_at_constitution_start: The acquisition bill was pending in the State Legislature when the Constitution commenced.
predicates.presidential_assent: The bill was reserved for and received the President’s assent.
predicates.constitutionally_protected_law: The law was among the laws protected by the constitutional provisions applicable to specified acquisition laws.

issues.definition: A challenge to compensation is barred when it concerns an acquisition law that was pending at the Constitution’s commencement, received presidential assent, and is constitutionally protected.

issues.legal_issue: The constitutional protection for specified acquisition laws does not bar judicial review of whether an acquisition is for a public purpose.
material_facts: The proprietors argued that the acquisition was not for a public purpose.
The Act had received the President’s assent and was included among the laws protected by the constitutional amendment.
issues.conclusion: A challenge that an acquisition lacks a public purpose remained open to judicial review notwithstanding the protections against compensation-based challenges.
issues.legal_principle: The majority of the Court treated the existence of a public purpose as a distinct requirement from the express compensation requirements of article 31(2). Article 31(4) barred challenges concerning the express compensation provisions, but did not bar review of whether the acquisition served a public purpose. The dissenting judges took a broader view of the bar; the majority’s ruling was that public purpose remained reviewable.

predicates.acquisition_law_challenge: A party challenged a law authorizing compulsory acquisition of property.
predicates.protected_acquisition_law: The acquisition law was protected from specified constitutional challenges.
predicates.challenge_based_on_absence_of_public_pur: The challenger alleged that the acquisition was not for a public purpose.

issues.definition: Even when an acquisition law is protected against other constitutional challenges, a claim that it lacks a public purpose may be reviewed.

issues.legal_issue: Acquiring estates to eliminate intermediaries, reform land distribution, and bring occupants into direct relations with the State serves a public purpose.
material_facts: The Act sought to abolish zamindari and other proprietary interests, eliminate intermediaries, and bring occupants into direct relations with the Government.
The reform was directed at changing the distribution and control of land and other material resources for the community’s benefit.
issues.conclusion: The acquisition of estates under the land-reform scheme was for a public purpose.
issues.legal_principle: The requirement of public purpose is assessed in light of the general interest of the community and the social conditions at the time of the legislation. The Court relied on the constitutional objectives in articles 38 and 39, including distributing material resources to serve the common good and preventing concentration of wealth. It referred to Hamabai Framjee Petit v. Secretary of State for India for the proposition that public purpose concerns the general interest of the community, while recognizing that the concept changes over time.

rule.if: estate_acquisition_case and (purpose_eliminates_intermediaries or purpose_reforms_land_distribution) and purpose_serves_general_community_interest

predicates.estate_acquisition_case: The proceeding concerns a law acquiring estates or comparable land interests.
predicates.purpose_eliminates_intermediaries: The law seeks to remove intermediaries between occupants and the State.
predicates.purpose_reforms_land_distribution: The law seeks to alter land distribution or control as part of a land-reform scheme.
predicates.purpose_serves_general_community_interes: The law’s objective is directed to the general benefit of the community rather than a private interest.

issues.definition: An estate acquisition serving land reform and the community’s general interest is an acquisition for a public purpose.

issues.legal_issue: A law that separately transfers pre-existing rent arrears to the State without a public purpose is unconstitutional.
material_facts: The Act transferred rent arrears due to proprietors for periods before the estates vested in the State.
The arrears were distinct from the land interests being acquired, and the State was to retain part of their value.
The majority found that taking the arrears did not further the land-reform purpose and instead served to augment State funds or finance compensation.
issues.conclusion: The provision acquiring the rent arrears was unconstitutional and void.
issues.legal_principle: Compulsory acquisition must serve a public purpose. The majority held that arrears of rent were a separate chose in action and that their transfer was not a necessary incident of the estate acquisition or the land-reform scheme. Article 31(4) did not bar review of the absence of a public purpose. Mukherjea J. additionally regarded the provision as a colourable device to deprive the owners of money without genuine compensation. The reasoning referred to the principles of eminent domain discussed in Cooley’s Constitutional Limitations and to the distinction between acquisition for public use and a forced loan.

rule.if: estate_acquisition_case and pre_existing_rent_debts_transferred_to_state and debts_separate_from_land_interests and no_public_purpose_for_debt_transfer

predicates.estate_acquisition_case: The proceeding concerns a law acquiring estates or comparable land interests.
predicates.pre_existing_rent_debts_transferred_to_s: The law transfers rent debts owed to former landholders to the State.
predicates.debts_separate_from_land_interests: The transferred debts arose independently of the land interests acquired by the State.
predicates.no_public_purpose_for_debt_transfer: The transfer of the debts does not serve a public purpose.

issues.definition: A separate transfer of pre-existing rent debts to the State is invalid when that transfer serves no public purpose.

issues.legal_issue: A fixed deduction for supposed works benefiting occupants is unconstitutional when it is an artificial device to reduce compensation rather than a genuine compensation principle.
material_facts: The Act deducted a percentage of gross assets for the supposed cost of works benefiting raiyats, without tying the deduction to actual expenditure.
The majority found that the deduction artificially reduced the compensation base and was not genuinely a principle for determining compensation.
issues.conclusion: The provision for the deduction was unconstitutional as colourable legislation.
issues.legal_principle: Entry 42 of List III authorizes legislation prescribing principles for determining compensation, but does not authorize a disguised device to reduce or defeat compensation. A legislature cannot achieve indirectly what it lacks power to do directly. The Court relied on South Australia v. The Commonwealth, Deputy Federal Commissioner of Taxation v. W. R. Moran Proprietary Ltd., and Madden v. Nelson & Fort Sheppard Railway Co. in considering colourable legislation.

predicates.acquisition_law_challenge: A party challenged a law authorizing compulsory acquisition of property.
predicates.compensation_based_on_asset_income: The law calculates compensation by reference to the income or assets of the property acquired.
predicates.deduction_for_beneficial_works_is_fixed_: The law deducts a set amount or percentage for beneficial works without linking it to actual costs incurred.
predicates.deduction_artificially_reduces_compensat: The deduction operates as a device to reduce compensation rather than to account for a genuine cost.

issues.definition: A fixed deduction disconnected from actual beneficial-works costs is invalid when it artificially reduces compensation.

issues.legal_issue: A legislature may leave the executive to determine details of compensation payment after the legislature has fixed the governing method and essential terms.
material_facts: The statute authorized compensation to be paid in cash, bonds, or a combination of both, specified the nature of the bonds and the instalment structure, and provided for interest.
The executive was left to determine the proportion payable in cash and bonds and the manner of payment, matters connected with the State’s available funds.
issues.conclusion: The delegation of those payment details to the State Government was valid and did not amount to an abdication of essential legislative power.
issues.legal_principle: The legislature may delegate details after settling the policy and essential principles of the law. The Court relied on The State of Bombay v. Narottamdas Jethabai and Queen v. Burah. It distinguished an impermissible transfer of essential legislative functions from a limited administrative discretion concerning implementation.

predicates.acquisition_law_challenge: A party challenged a law authorizing compulsory acquisition of property.
predicates.legislature_fixed_compensation_payment_o: The legislature specified the available forms of payment and the essential terms governing compensation.
predicates.executive_discretion_limited_to_payment_: The executive was left to decide implementation details such as the proportion and manner of payment.

issues.definition: Delegation is valid when the legislature fixes the essential compensation framework and leaves only payment details to the executive.

issues.legal_issue: A State law reserved for the President’s consideration and assented to by the President need not first receive the Governor’s assent to have effect under the constitutional requirement for acquisition laws.
material_facts: The State acquisition bills were passed by their respective State Legislatures and reserved by the Governors for the President’s consideration.
The challengers argued that the bills also required the Governors’ assent before presidential assent.
issues.conclusion: The constitutional requirement was satisfied by reservation of the bill and the President’s assent; an additional prior assent by the Governor was not required.
issues.legal_principle: Articles 31(3) and 200 contemplate reservation of a bill by the Governor for the President’s consideration without the Governor first assenting to it. The Court interpreted the constitutional references to a law and a bill in their procedural context and rejected the proposed requirement of two assents.

rule.if: state_acquisition_bill_challenged and bill_reserved_for_president and president_assented and challenge_requires_additional_governor_assent

predicates.state_acquisition_bill_challenged: A party challenged the validity of a State law authorizing compulsory acquisition.
predicates.bill_reserved_for_president: The State bill was reserved for the President’s consideration.
predicates.president_assented: The President assented to the reserved bill.
predicates.challenge_requires_additional_governor_a: The challenger claimed that the Governor must also have assented before the bill was reserved.

issues.definition: A reserved State acquisition bill that receives the President’s assent does not require an additional prior assent by the Governor.

issues.legal_issue: A failure to record the formal putting of a motion does not invalidate legislation when the authenticated bill establishes that it was passed and the omission is only a procedural irregularity.
material_facts: The official report of legislative proceedings did not record that the Speaker formally put the motion to pass the bill.
The authenticated bill bore the Speaker’s endorsement that the Assembly had passed it, and the proceedings showed no dissent to the motion.
issues.conclusion: The omission did not invalidate the Act; at most, it was an irregularity of legislative procedure.
issues.legal_principle: Article 212(1) bars courts from inquiring into legislative proceedings on the ground of an alleged irregularity of procedure. The authenticated bill and the Speaker’s endorsement supported the conclusion that the bill had been passed.

predicates.legislative_validity_challenge: A party challenged the validity of a law based on how the legislature conducted its proceedings.
predicates.authenticated_bill_records_passage: The bill authenticated by the presiding officer records that the legislature passed it.
predicates.only_defect_is_omitted_formal_record_of_: The asserted defect is only that the formal putting or recording of the motion is absent from the official proceedings.

issues.definition: A missing formal record of a vote does not invalidate a law when the authenticated bill records its passage and the defect is procedural.

issues.legal_issue: A constitutional provision specifically validating listed laws applies to a listed law even if the property acquired by that law does not fall within the separate constitutional definition of an estate.
material_facts: The Madhya Pradesh acquisition law was specifically listed among the laws protected by the constitutional amendment.
Some acquired malguzari lands were conceded not to be estates under the relevant local land-tenure law.
issues.conclusion: The specific validation of the listed law applied notwithstanding that the particular lands were not estates.
issues.legal_principle: Article 31-B independently validates the Acts and Regulations specified in the Ninth Schedule against challenges based on Part III; its application is not restricted to laws concerning estates under article 31-A. The opening words of article 31-B preserve the generality of article 31-A rather than narrowing the specific validation in article 31-B.

predicates.acquisition_law_challenge: A party challenged a law authorizing compulsory acquisition of property.
predicates.law_specifically_listed_for_constitution: The law was specifically named in a constitutional schedule validating specified laws.
predicates.acquired_property_not_an_estate: The particular property acquired does not qualify as an estate under the applicable local land-tenure law.

issues.definition: Specific constitutional validation of a listed law applies even when the acquired property is not an estate.

issues.legal_issue: Acquiring property recognized as a former ruler’s private property under a merger covenant does not, without more, breach the ruler’s constitutional guarantees when the property is acquired in the same capacity as other private property.
material_facts: The properties had been recognized as the former rulers’ private property under merger arrangements.
The acquisition laws acquired those properties as private property and provided for compensation on that basis.
issues.conclusion: The acquisition did not contravene the asserted guarantee concerning the rulers’ personal rights or assurances under the merger arrangements.
issues.legal_principle: The Court treated acquisition of recognized private property in the same manner as other privately owned property as distinct from a breach of a guarantee preserving the ruler’s personal rights. It also noted the limits on judicial intervention in disputes concerning merger covenants and related agreements.

predicates.acquisition_law_challenge: A party challenged a law authorizing compulsory acquisition of property.
predicates.property_recognized_as_former_ruler_priv: The property had been recognized as the private property of a former ruler under a merger arrangement.
predicates.acquired_in_same_capacity_as_other_priva: The State acquired the property in its capacity as private property and on the same basis as other privately owned property.

issues.definition: Acquisition of property recognized as a former ruler’s private property does not breach a merger guarantee when it is acquired in the same capacity as other private property.
